bull.b: Atlassian combines recurring cloud subscriptions with exceptionally high gross margins, supporting durable economics as customers expand usage. The cloud mix and strong unit economics provide a foundation for reinvestment in product development, sales capacity, and AI capabilities while preserving substantial cash conversion.

bull.t: Strong and growing free cash flow
bull.b: Robust operating and free cash flow demonstrates that Atlassian converts its subscription revenue into cash despite reported accounting losses. This internally generated funding supports product investment, customer expansion, and strategic flexibility, while reducing reliance on external capital over the next several quarters.

bull.t: Enterprise expansion and durable customer retention
bull.b: High net revenue retention and sharply rising remaining performance obligations indicate customers are expanding their commitments rather than merely renewing. Growth in large-account cohorts strengthens Atlassian’s enterprise position, raises recurring revenue visibility, and creates additional cross-sell potential across its platform.

bear.t: GAAP losses and uneven operating profitability
bear.b: Persistent GAAP losses and volatile operating profitability show that strong gross margins have not yet translated consistently into bottom-line earnings. Continued cost pressure could limit the pace at which cash generation becomes accounting profit and may constrain confidence in the durability of operating leverage.

bear.t: Moderating FY27 growth and margin guidance
bear.b: Management’s lower ARR growth outlook indicates that the unusually strong expansion rate is expected to moderate over the coming fiscal year. The reduced full-year margin guide also implies continued investment and execution demands, making sustained growth and profitability improvement less certain.

bear.t: Meaningful leverage remains on the balance sheet
bear.b: Although leverage has improved materially from earlier years, debt still exceeds equity and operating cash flow covers only about 38% of total debt. This leaves less financial flexibility than a lightly levered software model and could compete with growth investment if profitability remains weak.
